To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the area of an inscribed polygon can be approximated by the area of a circumscribed polygon of the same number of sides, and that the difference between the two areas is the sum of the areas of the triangles formed by connecting the vertices of the circumscribed polygon to the center of the circle.

1) a minimum-problem for inscribed and circuinscribed polygons of a given circle can be solved in a closed form; 2) the minimum area of an inscribed polygon is equal to the area of a regular hexagon; and 3) the minimum area is achieved by a polygon of 24 sides.

(1) the minimum problem on the area of an n-gon inscribed in and circumscribed about a circle has a unique solution for all n > 3; and (2) the solution for the area of the inscribed polygon can be expressed in terms of the solution for the circumscribed polygon, and vice versa, by means of a simple algebraic formula.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the area of the smallest polygon circumscribing a circle of given area, or the area of the largest polygon inscribed in a circle of given circumference.

the following questions: (i) What is the minimum number of sides of a polygon inscribed in a circle, or circumscribed around a circle, such that the area of the polygon is greater than a given positive real number?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the area of any inscribed or circumscribed polygon is always less than the area of a circle and greater than the area of the circle, respectively.
, if a circle is inscribed in a polygon, the area of the circumscribing polygon is greater than that of the inscribed polygon by an amount equal to the area of the circle.
the area of the inscribed polygon of n sides is less than the area of the circumscribed polygon of n + 2 sides.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown how to construct an algorithm that, for any given polygonal domain, computes the area of the domain in time O(n2 log n), where n is the number of vertices of the polygon.
we show that the problem of finding the minimum of a polynomial function of a real variable is equivalent to the problem of finding a local minimum of a polynomial in several complex variables.
we have shown that the area of the inscribed polygon is always larger than the area of the circumscribed polygon.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the problem of finding a minimum-area circumscribed polygon of a convex shape is NP-hard in the worst case, but it can be solved in polynomial time for some special cases.
the minimum-problem on the areas of inscribed polygons of a given circle can be solved by the use of a simple geometric construction.
we can use a minimum-problem on the areas of polygons inscribed and circumscripted to a circle to derive the formula for the area of a circle.
